They were qualified to carry out the security assessment and to do everything else that is required by the assessment of the situation to prepare the combat, to issue his decision. And this is all very clear and all the officers are aware of all this. They're familiar with the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. Now, the next point that you were questioned on was this report, the Dzankovic report, which was MFI221. That was shown to you. And you replied somewhere there, you said, "Maybe pursuant to Mr. Halilovic's instructions these proposals were made by Dzankovic. Do you remember that? Or do you -- any time, Mr. Jasarevic, you want to see a particular document, please be free to ask, and I will show it to you. But if you remember, you may answer.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was probably said in that sense, and I'll try and answer your question. Mr. Dzankovic was subordinate to Mr. Halilovic as a member of the inspection team. In that sense, the -- it was the authority and the right of Mr. Halilovic to decide which tasks he would give to the members of the inspection team in keeping with his authorities, as stipulated in the order that determined the tasks of the inspection team. And nobody else could influence that, when we're talking about issuing orders to Dzankovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the other -- the other -- your other evidence is that these were unrealistic proposals which had been put forward by Dzankovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you said there you see no realistic possibility for Dzankovic to do anything without clear orders from a position of authority. That was one of the -- one of the utterances you made, is that -- do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the context. In my view, from the aspect of my professional mandate, Dzankovic was not the person who could carry out such complex tasks in such a complex situation without having resources at his disposal. When I say "resources," I mean officers of the military security such as were available to aid either a brigade or a corps. Further on, he should have had police officers, strong forces that were necessary in order to carry out an investigation and collection of relevant information that would enable for the proceedings to go on. That's one element. The second element is Dzankovic's mandate as a member of the inspection team. If I understand the principles of inspection well and the principles of an inspection team as such, I would say that this is a body of control. Dzankovic, as a member of the inspection team, could to a certain extent oversee the work of a certain service, of certain units, and so on and so forth, which would have been involved in such an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said he did not have the resources -- without resources. But who could have ordered these resources? Was there anyone who could have actually ordered these resources?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a formal sense, I don't recognise such persons. I have spoken at great length about that. I was not on the ground. I was not familiar with the important elements that came into play in that operation such as the organisational order that should have preceded such an operation, the decision of the commander or order, which depended on the level of the -- the operation, any annexes to such an order that might have been drafted. For example, plans, proposals, tasks to subordinate units. And this is all what I refer to as a very thick file. And if one looked at such a file, one would be very clear on what the tasks were if anything unforeseen had happened, such as was the crime that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I'm not asking you for a name of a person. All I'm saying is in military doctrinal terms who could have ordered resources? Dzankovic couldn't. Who could have? Dzankovic being replaced by military security officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think there's a confusion here between the concrete case and the theory. My friend is telling the witness that she wants a theoretical answer but she keeps relating it back to Mr. Dzankovic. Now, if it's a concrete-case answer that she wants, then she's got it. But -- and if it's a theoretical-case answer that she wants, then that should be made clear because the two can't be mixed in one answer, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And in the answer of this witness, the witness said, "When I say'resources,' I mean officers of the military security such as were available to aid either a brigade or a corps." Do you mean the resources like this?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Any -- let's clarify from the witness. Resources and who -- he said he did not have the resources, who could have ordered these resources, whatever they may be, Your Honour. And I did -- and I did correct it by saying "replace Mr. Dzankovic with a military security officer." So it's a -- it's not -- may I ask...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I'm just asking you in military doctrinal terms, if a military officer in the same situation as Dzankovic, who would have been in a position to order these resources for this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was very clear, perhaps a little too detailed in the explanation of this question. If we have a command and a commander, then there is no dilemma there. Those persons would order the commander or the command organs then would implement it. The whole time I don't see the command. I don't know who the commander is. And I cannot give you a quality answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to another topic, and this is a document which you were shown, MFI222, which is the report of Salihamidzic. Sorry, I'm sure I'm pronouncing that horribly. This is in respect of the Karic words. And you said -- and you were asked about that at some length. And I think you said that Karic was a person of good moral character and you cannot assume that he would say such a thing. Do you remember that, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer, Mr. Jasarevic. The interpreter did not get your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, this -- these words, they were reflected in that particular report, were they not? You saw them?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is there any reason for you to assume that he did not -- that he in fact -- can you rule out the possibility that he said these things, these words, about throwing the Croatian civilians into the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that I expressed my opinion clearly on this matter, and I'm stating it now. Only in a situation that was not normal -- or only if Mr. Karic was not in his usual state of mind could I expect such a statement from Mr. Karic. But if he was in his usual, normal state of mind, I don't think that he would be capable of saying anything like that. But then, as I say, I didn't see it, I didn't hear it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, going back to Dzankovic again. You were shown Article 40 of the rules, and it came in the context of that. And you said that "Dzankovic had no competence, no authority, no power. He never received an order from a commander. He could see these -- to see these things through." Do you remember that, saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that sense, yes. But I was supposed to receive the order, as the person in charge of the administration, so that I could give my subordinates their tasks. That was one option. The other option was for the superiors of certain organs of the command to receive certain orders. And there is a definite procedure on how this is done. In this case, I didn't see anything like that and I don't know whether Dzankovic did or did not, but I don't think that he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was -- remind us, Mr. Jasarevic. Who was Dzankovic's superior? Who was he subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the inspection team you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Who was he subordinated to? Was he anywhere else other than the inspection team at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His superior --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that -- that last question reflects, in my respectful submission -- I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, you may answer that question. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the order of the commander on the establishment and composition of the inspection team, the superior of Mr. Dzankovic was Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, this is in respect of MFI233 that you were shown, and this was your own report, dated 21st September, which was a response to Dzankovic's report. And you said that you gave him some realistic jobs to do. Do you remember that, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, in response to these realistic jobs that you gave him, were -- do you know whether any investigations or any arrests or any convictions occurred in respect of these matters?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the field during the Neretva 93 operation?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, did anything happen, to your knowledge? You can talk about the field. You can -- you can talk about afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I don't think the interpreter got your answer. Would you please repeat it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted a clarification of whether you were thinking of the duration of the Neretva 93 operation or the location where the operation was carried out. So I received the answer yes, and I will give you my reply now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can see it from Dzankovic's report on the 10th of October to me that there were no arrests or any investigations or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. I would like to take you to this document that you were shown. And this is MFI235.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd appreciate it if you did bring that up on the screen, court orderly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, this is the document you were shown by learned Defence counsel, and it has the names of 30 people who had been massacred in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, not who were massacred but those who lived in Grabovica before the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the number "30", you can see that the word there is "zivelo," lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for that, Mr. Jasarevic. I stand completely correct. Because the following document says: "The following 30 persons lived in the Grabovica area when the massacre of Croatian civilians took place." Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when you were shown the last paragraph of that particular document - and you may look at it again - you said that 20 days -- this was after 20 days after the crime had been committed and it was impossible not to stop the combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jasarevic. I'm sorry if -- you did say that it was 20 days afterwards and it was impossible not to stop the combat activity. Now, which particular combat activity are we talking about? Can you please clarify that first.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand from the report that there are combat activities. Practically in every report the main focus is that question. You cannot do such-and-such a thing concerning actual elements of the inquiry because that would bring into question the planned combat activities. This is what I meant. I wasn't in the field in order to be able to determine the places, the time, and the forces which continued with the combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when you said "20 days -- this was 20 days after," is there anything -- why -- why did you mention that it was 20 days after? And the sentence is "it is impossible to get statements from perpetrators or identify them because they returned to Sarajevo immediately after the operation at Vrdi and are no longer in these areas." Did you -- do you mean it was too late after 20 days?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'm -- what I'm thinking of are the eyewitnesses who had left that area. Especially of interest were the civilians, those who -- well, different terms were used here, who were brought out, evacuated, escorted, accommodated to -- at some premises in Jablanica and so on and so forth. I'm thinking of the citizens, the civilians of the village of Grabovica, other eyewitnesses, other possible eyewitnesses are the units which were located there, and I'm thinking of the unit of the 2nd Independent Battalion, sections of that unit, and units or sections of the 9th Motorised Brigade from Sarajevo. Because in this period when Dzankovic sent this report to me, he notes it well that there are no such eyewitnesses out in the field and that it was impossible to work with them, to take statements, make arrests, and so on, what needed to be done in the terms of the police work, when we're talking about an investigation of a crime like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What about the perpetrators, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they are at that time. I don't know if they're still in combat, if they're in Sarajevo, because this is already a 20-day period. And he says here that they returned. But we received the document on the 10th of October. It was written on the 29th of September though. So a lot of time has passed by in order to be able to locate any particular moment specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could this then have been done earlier, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to that. Your Honours, this is now an attempt to lead evidence in chief on matters that if the Prosecutor wanted to do it should have led it in chief and exposed the situation for me to then cross-examine about, if needs be. But the witness -- the Prosecution now, having seen what's unfolded, is attempting to commence again. I'd submit this is clearly evidence-in-chief material. This question shouldn't be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, but I believe that this is a follow-up question with a question in the cross-examination. So we'll allow it, this question to go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, could this then have been done earlier, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider this to be a crucial question. And in my profound conviction, this should have been done absolutely, immediately, because we know what time means in investigations, in circumstances such as these. We have a situation which could then provide faithful elements, which could then be later used in a criminal proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: There is one last question on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you look at the front -- the first page of this document, Mr. Jasarevic. Is it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you -- can you read for me, please, when it says "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." What does it say under that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "IKM," which is an abbreviation for a forward command post, "For the Supreme Command Staff, SVK, Jablanica, on the 29th of September, 1993." This is if you're thinking of the upper left-hand corner --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So this is the IKM in Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it states here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you have seen this document before. I believe you said that you had.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what was this IKM post in Jablanica, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but the question is not clear enough to me. Are you asking me what that means, "forward command post, IKM," or what kind of a forward command post there was in Jablanica? The question is not clear, so if you can please clarify it for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The latter, Mr. Jasarevic. What kind of a forward command post was there in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I placed in question the existence at all of that command, of that organ, based on information which I received later. I didn't see any documents that would indicate that there really was a forward command post. I'm thinking of a document bearing the authority of the commander and so on. Except for the reports which arrived from the ground, which came to my hands, all of them bore this heading "Forward command post." I wanted to be as fair as possible or precise as possible. And this can be also termed in jargon. Wherever there was a group of superior officers conducting a series of activities with elements of command, control, of some military activities or control, then this would somehow be termed as a forward command post. However, if you look at the rules, a forward command post is something completely different; it's a more powerful organ with the elements of command. And for a short period of time it's relocated, transferred to some other location for practical reasons. I tried to clarify this in terms of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jasarevic. Now, that is all I have from you other than to thank you very much for your patience?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Witness, I will be very brief and I would seek some clarification concerning two or three matters. First of all, if I understood you well, in answer to a question put to you, you said- I'm quoting you- "I don't see that Mr. Sefer Halilovic is the commander of the operation." And you were commenting the order of August 1993 establishing, as you know, the inspection team. I want you, please, if you can, to be more explicit in explaining how and why did you come to this conclusion, the conclusion being that Mr. Halilovic is not in your opinion the commander of the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to allocate a superior officer as commander of an operation, there should be a clear order in that sense. This order should set out a number of details amongst which also the commander. The order that I gave my comments on is absolutely clear that it is inaugurating an inspection team. All the superior officers and all of those who are dealing with military organisation are quite clear on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: So you came to the conclusion on the face of the language of the order of -- of August 1993, if I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the second part of my answer, that it's the inspection teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: So my second question will be: If an operation is underway supposedly under the command of the Chief of Staff, would it be necessary to give you information in view of your position about the operation and, if any, a post of commander of the -- the conduct of the operation known as the IKM? Would it be necessary militarily speaking that you be informed about an operation under the command of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the sixth element of combat readiness is security and self-protection, implying the function of securing combat security as an element of combat readiness. In the evaluation of a situation during preparation of combat activities or the operation, in this case, the military security service must participate so that it can carry out this task, the one that is termed "the element of combat readiness." So in that function, it would be essential for them to be acquainted about this. I'm thinking about the military security organ. Which organ this would be would be something that would be regulated by the order, in the organisational sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: But normally, in normal, I would say, circumstances, do you suggest that you should be informed to secure security?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I myself or somebody from the security service who is competent to carry out such a task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Yes. And you don't know if ever Mr. Halilovic asked that security be provided for the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question, please, is about the behaviour of the 9th and the 10th Brigades. If I understand you well, this was the subject of a meeting of the committee to the protection of the constitution. And you were present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: At the same meeting, Mr. Delic explained that he tried to bring the 10th Brigade to discipline but his efforts were not successful.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Did he suggest any matter concerning this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot remember specifically these measures, but I know that it was requested that a position be taken at the highest level on the resolution of that question in view of the issue of the defence of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: So what do you mean by "the highest authority," or "the highest level," since Mr. Delic was present?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm thinking of -- of the position of the Presidency as the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Okay. So this leads me to the other question: You said that generally speaking these two brigades were populated by good soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, this is the reason why they were entrusted to the defence of the town, and it's common knowledge the importance of the town as a symbol to the -- to the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: So in case that a similar operation of a similar importance is to be conducted, as a military man do you see any inconvenience to seek the efforts of well-trained, as you put it, "good soldiers" to accomplish the other operation? And I have in mind the operation to secure road and to regain the city of Mostar. For you -- as I understand, you were one of the inner circle of the -- at the top level of the military, and for sure you have an idea about the importance of the city of Mostar. So in case of a decision that this city be liberated, as a military man aware of all the circumstances and the events that -- that were occurring by or inside these two brigades, would you consider a decision to seek help of these two brigades, a sound military decision?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if anyone were to ask me for my opinion, I would not propose the use of those brigades for that task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Can you give a short explanation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation is as follows: We already had information that there were individuals in those brigades whose conduct was undisciplined and that this lack of discipline was quite pronounced, and that is the main reason. Of course, I would not be able to foresee anything that happened with this, but it would be sufficient for me not to propose and not to take upon such a risk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with the most important operation, I mean, the defence of the city of Sarajevo. And you said yourself that they -- in general they were good soldiers. I mean -- my question was: If you need some good soldiers, can you go and fetch them from these two brigades; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question is about the recruitment of the personnel to the army. You explained that at the very beginning there was no army and that the establishment of the army took place during the -- the conflict itself. So on what basis the recruitment was founded? I mean if a call to every and all able men or able persons to join the army? Was this the method?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain regulations were issued on the state of war being proclaimed and on mobilisation, so it was regulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: No. To be more clear, I'm -- I was -- I had in mind the able men or able persons that some of -- members of the two -- or I think mainly the 10th Brigade, that they forced them to dig trenches, saying that they are cellar dwellers, as you put it, I think. So I mean, if these -- or whether these persons, you know, in the streets not joining the army, are they obedient to orders or can you come to a conclusion that they were exempted from the military service, for example, or that somebody for some reason did not join the -- the army because it was -- it was a popular army, if I understand, in the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, absolutely

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: And everybody -- if I may say, everybody in the city, in -- in the circumstances of the case, was supposed to participate, whether in the civil activity or in the military activity. The city was under siege; yes, I think. For -- for more than -- it's common knowledge, for at least some two years. So in your opinion, these persons not joining the army, staying in the city, not contributing to the military activities or the military effort or to the -- to the war effort, how do you judge them? What's your opinion about them?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city of Sarajevo was under siege for three and a half years. These individuals who fell under the category, as you explained, this cannot be considered as characteristic. I probably used the term conditionally. When I call them "cellar mice" or "cellar dwellers," among them there were those individuals who had professional obligations and who had other tasks to perform. In order for the life to function in the city, there had to be all sorts of people of all sorts of walks of life and who did those jobs. Some people were also on leave, and at that time they wore civilian clothes. Again, I'm going to use the term "conditionally." Those who gathered these people and who took them to the lines to dig trenches, they did not check why those people were not on the lines already. I do not exclude the possibility that some pulled some strings and resorted to -- to some dishonest methods to avoid being sent to the lines, but their numbers were negligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of judge's question? I see -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just clarify one very small matter coming out of Judge El Mahdi's questions, and that is in respect of the defence of Sarajevo. I just -- from what I read in the transcript, it appeared to me that the 9th or the 10th were the only troops participating in the defence of Sarajevo. I just -- I just thought that it should be clarified whether it was, you know, them holding a part of the line or other troops. I don't know whether Judge El Mahdi would like that to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you can do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasarevic, just one small clarification coming from the Honourable Judge El Mahdi's question. How many troops were surrounding Sarajevo? How many troops for the whole portion of the city? And what portion was the 9th and 10th holding?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo you meant, I suppose. Question? Yes? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I understood your question. Your Honours, there were over ten brigades at times that defended Sarajevo. There were some smaller unit, detachments. The line of defence around Sarajevo was rather long, and it engaged quite a number of units. However, these two brigades occupied a very prominent position in the defence of Sarajevo because those were very strong units and they were positioned one across each other. The 10th, for example, defended the southern part of the city, and it was engaged in combat almost every day. The 9th was engaged in the northern part of the defence line, and it was also engaged in very intense fighting against the enemy. When their mission was jeopardised, and if it had been jeopardised, this would have meant a disaster for the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, are there any documents to tender? Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we have put in a list this morning with all the documents that I used during the testimony of Mr. Jasarevic. And we have sent them to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Like you ordered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are some objections. I raised the possibility yesterday and -- of dealing with this by motion, but I can indicate that my objections to the Prosecution documents can be dealt with now orally, if you would like me to. Is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, just point out which documents that you have objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Could I indicate there's two levels of objection. And if I do it in a general level, that will save me doing document by document, which is going to take a long time. I have an objection generally on the grounds of remoteness to the operative-information documents, because we say that the evidence as it currently stands goes no further than saying that Mr. Jasarevic himself, as -- and we haven't challenged him in any way on this, so we receive that he received operative information and so on. But Mr. Jasarevic isn't on trial; Mr. Halilovic is. And the Prosecution didn't seek to show or didn't try to show how this material was -- came to the attention of -- of Halilovic. Not only did the evidence not come out, but there really wasn't an effort made to get it. So for that reason, I'd submit it's all just not sufficiently connected to the case to be admitted into evidence at all. It's effectively irrelevant. That's a general objection that applies to all of the operative-information documents. A more specific objection arises with respect to the MUP documents, and I can -- I'll enumerate those briefly. MFI204, 205, 210,-- I might just list these for the transcript. The same basic argument applies to all of these. 212, but I want to make the point that 212 is slightly different for a reason I'll come to in a moment. And 218 as well. Other documents, whilst we have objections to them, as arising from the MUP, were operative information that passed through this witness's hands, and so if you're against me on my first objection, the general one, then those -- then those documents would then be admitted into evidence. These ones are a bit different because these are ones that the witness himself said he never did see. And there needs to be some sense of predictabilty about when documents like that will be admit, which applies both to the Defence and to the Prosecutor, the Defence having put forward some documents as well which need to be analysed in somewhat the same way, although the standard is different when you're cross-examining, as Your Honour knows. Nevertheless, it still remains that the Defence must abide by the Rules, as the Prosecutor must. And what I'd submit is an appropriate way to deal with these documents in this way is this: Firstly, everything I say is within the context of the clear -- of the guidelines that Your Honours gave at the start of the case, which are an order of the Court, I don't seek to transverse those. Secondly, where a document has passed through the witness's hands and he's looked at it, then that is a powerful matter in favour of admitting the document. And that's the case whether or not the information in the document is true, reliable, or otherwise. Secondly, it may be possible to admit a document even if the witness hasn't seen it because he's professionally able to comment upon it. An example of that would be a report going through the SVB line, this military security line, which this witness may or may not have seen but can comment that it arrived in the system in a particular way, and so on. And I acknowledge that that would be a reason to admit it. And then the question of its weight arises at a later time, of course. I do make this point as well: That where a document has absolutely unmeasurable weight - in other words, when it can't be determined whether it's got weight or not - that is a question of weight but it's also a question of admissibility, because if a document is incapable of being assessed for weight, then it's a waste of the Court's time and it really does apply to the question of its admissibility as well as your assessment of it later. There's a practical reason for that. It clutters the court record, frankly. But -- you know, there's a theoretical reason behind it too. It can't help, so it shouldn't be admitted. It's incapable of helping, so it can't be admitted. Now, with those general comments in mind, I and it that the information that Mr. Jasarevic was shown that came from the MUP but he didn't say had passed before him should clearly not be admitted. Information that came through his own service, even if he didn't see it, it would be appropriate to admit it in those circumstances. This is, of course, subject to if I fail on my general application, my first application. This is now dealing with specifics. Therefore, documents -- sorry, 204, 205, 210, 212, and 218 ought to all not be admitted for that reason. Now, in respect of all of those except 212, the Prosecutor asked the witness, and quite rightly, I indicate, whether or not he'd seen the document. The proofing notes revealed the situation and we all knew what the position was, and the Prosecutor nevertheless showed the document to the witness. 212, I think in evidence -- I couldn't find the part in the transcript, but I think, I have to concede, my recollection is that he did say that he'd seen it or he might have seen it. I just can't recall, I'm sorry to say. But I -- rather than hide behind ignorance as a weapon. I think I'd better admit that that's the fact, that I think he said it. It might well be that he saw it. So that's -- I'm being asked to slow down and I'm grateful for that indication. The other buns, I indicate that as a second line of defence with respect to all of them, I'd submit that where he hasn't seen it or where his service didn't receive it or have any reason to know about it, then those documents shouldn't be admitted. There are other situations in which documents can be admitted, of course, outside of that, but I'm just dealing with the situation as to my friend's documents. Having said that, there's one ore matter to raise. Of course there are some documents in there which are entirely uncontroversial. The organigramme, which is 212, is not objected to, naturally. And there is one other which -- I'm sorry, if Your Honour would just excuse me a moment. I will attempt to indicate a cooperative attitude. Obviously 213, 214, and 215 are all not objected to on any ground on any basis and can be admitted immediately. Those are the submissions I have in relation to the residual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I believe that taking into consideration of this late hour, I believe that we could admit the documents 202, 206, 207, 208, 209, 211, 213, 214, 216, 217. And as for the other documents, we'll consider the objections from the Defence and try to make it in a written form. If during the meantime the parties would like to submit their reasons in written form, that will be welcomed. As for the document 215, I think the Defence also submitted a document with another number, that is, 221. I believe that we have said it very clear that if one document, we'd better have one number on it. So I hope that after this sitting the parties will discuss this matter together and try to come to a common kind of agreed translation or document on this issue. It is so decided. Are there any documents on the Defence side that you would like to tender at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, there is a large number of documents that the Defence wishes to tender. I believe that the -- before court proceedings today, we gave a -- a lengthy list of documents that was incomplete, pending what was to be advanced in cross-examination this afternoon. And now we have the -- the document. May I inquire of the Court and of the Prosecutors whether we have all the same thing; namely, a -- a list of 29 potential documents to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I have 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, no, no, 28, Your Honour. I'm sorry. There was a -- in reality, it's 27 because, as you'll see, the headings section has got a number in our numbering system. So I apologise for that. So it really is 27, and the last page seems to be an extra document, but it's not. So 27 documents all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any objections to those 27 documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in normal circumstance it is Prosecution is guided by your rules on the admissibility of evidence, and in these -- those terms, of course there will be no objections. But I find it rather curious that the Defence now seeks to admit into evidence documents by the very same witness from these organisations but the witness said he hasn't seen these this is document before. I think there should be one consistent rule. That would be my point. And if the Defence exhibits are admitted on those bases, I say that the Prosecution's should be. And I think both parties should be -- should continue to be guided by the practice directions that Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- were so kind to give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. I'm asking you a specific question: Which documents you agree and which you have objections on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment I have still not given detailed consideration to this -- this list, because it just arrived today. I've already indicated about that in the transcript. One has to look at it a little more carefully. Would it be all right with Your Honours if we were to indicate this in writing as to which ones we object to and which ones we don't by Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. Of course. I'm just trying to facilitate the procedures, you know. But if you are not ready for that, I believe that you are allowed to submit in written form concerning all the documents listed in this list. And we'll consider it together with the left over documents in your list.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. I'm sorry that we kept you in The Hague so long. I believe that you miss your home. So Madam Usher will show you out of the room during the break, and it's high time for us to have a break, so we'll have 20 minutes' break and we'll resume at 6.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's come to the next witness. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have a -- some motions first, two motions. Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, while that's being done, I wish to raise another abundance of caution matter. I just didn't see on the transcript. Was a pseudonym granted to this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, the pseudonym and facial distortion. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: With an abundance of caution, I welcome any warnings to me because I just had slip-ups on the last occasion and I -- I take very seriously what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We plan on referring to this witness as "E," as in "Edward."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For clarification, it's pseudonym and facial distortion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please made the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first may I explain to the witness what we're going to be doing today, because I explained to him previously that there were various options of giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness E, I was just going to tell you that we had talked about various options of giving your evidence. We're going to go through all your evidence from start to finish orally. Do you understand? We're not going to hand in your reports.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in front of you is a sheet of paper. And could you look at the first line in the middle. It's -- and is that your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The second line, is that your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, the third line, is that your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could that be shown to the Defence and then I'd like to offer it and ask that it be sealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to tender it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I guess there's no objections with this piece of paper. So it's admitted into the evidence. Madam Court Deputy will pronounce a number to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is marked as 245.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we go into some -- into private session to briefly go through some background, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In the fall of 1993, where was your unit located, Witness E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Our base was on the Faculty of Dentistry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did something happen at that time, during the fall, that changed you being in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We were sent into the field, to Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to being sent to Grabovica, were you called to gather? Were you given any instructions? Did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The commander assembled us and told us that we were going into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you why you were going to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: For -- in order to liberate Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you the name of this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what would happen once you got to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Through the tunnel and then by buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you eventually arrive in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately the time of day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: At noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were there -- were there any people living in Grabovica when you arrived? Were there any inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: When we arrived, there were the inhabitants there. They were a little afraid because the soldiers had arrived, but this fear disappeared quite quickly because we shared with them cigarettes, coffee, whatever we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And of what ethnic group were the people who inhabited Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us about the age level of these inhabitants that you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In their -- they were in their 50s and 60s.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, where did you stay when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We found accommodation in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did everyone in your unit stay in the same house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you stay and with whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: With Igor Martinovic, Nijaz Kremo [phoen], Emir Kapo, Emir Muslic, Zoran Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what did you do when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: What do you mean what did we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, did you go right into battle? Did you do other things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. We rested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you partake of any other activities after resting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you and the members of your unit do? Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We were sent to Medved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, the first few days before you were sent to Medved, let's talk about -- in relation to the water, what, if anything, did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do in relation to the water or the river? Well, let me ask it this way: Did anyone go swimming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Any other water activities? Was there any fishing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, we did some fishing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you relaxed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with two other brigades, Celo's and Caco's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see either of those units in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's the time-honoured problem of putting those two together. My friend did, and I acknowledge, use the word "either of those units." But an answer of yes -- a simple answer of yes might be misleading to that one, so if it could be taken step by step, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was planning to do that. That was the opening question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But -- well, I think it's almost time. Shall we stop here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why don't we break here, Your Honour. That would be good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, I understand that you have been here for a long time, but we have to keep you here during the weekend. Now your status is different as before because you are under the oath, so do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes., I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after the court adjourns, the usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a happy weekend in The Hague. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
